children: President
Donald Trump

signed an executive order late Friday requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House before responding to congressional inquiries involving their work with the executive branch.
It directs them to follow the administration’s instructions on withholding communications it considers protected by executive privilege.
The order warns that companies failing to comply could face contract termination or suspension and debarment from future federal work, reported the Associated Press.
Democrats To Take Control Of Congress
Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January and have promised aggressive investigations into the administration, Trump’s family business activity and ties to private firms.
The move lands as
in an Emerson College poll and after Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms.
New Gatekeeping Step
For contractors, the directive creates a new gatekeeping step between congressional requests and any response, potentially slowing document production and witness preparation.

That fight is intensifying as Democrats prepare to use committee powers to examine conflicts of interest, federal contracting decisions, immigration enforcement and the administration’s handling of the
Jeffrey Epstein

investigation. In the Emerson poll, voters’ views of the parties also shifted, with 44% rating Democrats favorably versus 47% unfavorably, while Republicans drew a 35% favorable and 56% unfavorable split.

The same order threatens real financial consequences for businesses that rely on government revenue, tying compliance to eligibility for federal dollars. That economic leverage comes as voters put pressure on lawmakers to focus on household finances, with 57% naming cost of living as a top priority for Congress in 2027.
Earlier in the week, White House Counsel
Will Scharf

issued guidance telling federal agencies to get White House sign-off before employees agree to testify, according to Reuters. Scharf argued some Democratic investigative efforts could cross into criminal conduct, a stance that drew scrutiny over whether the administration is trying to narrow oversight tools.
How Voter Sentiment Shapes Political Tactics

The polling picture helps explain why the administration may be trying to control information flows before committees flip hands. Emerson found Trump at 37% approval, down from 39% in September, while disapproval measured 54%, down from 58%.

Party images moved over the past year as well, with Democrats’ favorable rating rising nine points while Republicans’ favorable rating fell nine points and their unfavorable rating climbed 12 points. Those trendlines include responses from Democrats, Republicans and independents, suggesting the coming oversight cycle will play out in a politically charged environment.
Democrats have already begun laying groundwork for document battles. Rep.
Robert Garcia
(D-Calif.), who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent preservation letters to 12 people tied to Trump, including family members and senior current and former officials.
Garcia’s list included White House Chief of Staff
Stephen Miller
, Vice President
JD Vance
, Attorney General
Todd Blanche
and former White House Chief of Staff
Susie Wiles
White House Defends Order

The White House defended the order as a way to protect sensitive communications, including national security-related material, and warned that contractors acting on their own could trigger expensive court disputes, as reported by Reuters. The administration has also argued executive privilege can cover exchanges with outside advisers even when those advisers are not government employees.

The order could invite legal challenges if contractors are directed to withhold material sought through congressional subpoenas, potentially setting up disputes over Congress’ investigative authority and the administration’s claims of executive privilege.
